items.title: The travel rule, in plain terms
items.body: FATF's 'travel rule' requires virtual asset service providers to pass along originator and beneficiary information (name, account number, sometimes address) on transfers above a jurisdiction's threshold — mirroring rules that have existed in traditional wire transfers for decades. It's the main reason exchange-to-exchange transfers increasingly carry more metadata than a wallet-to-wallet move.

items.title: Stablecoins aren't all backed the same way
items.body: Fiat-collateralized stablecoins (like USDC, USDT) hold reserves off-chain in cash and short-term securities; crypto-collateralized ones (like DAI) are over-collateralized by on-chain assets to absorb price swings; algorithmic designs try to hold a peg through incentives alone with no hard collateral — the last category has the worst historical track record for depegging under stress.

items.title: Why mixers don't fully break traceability
items.body: Tools like coin mixers and privacy pools break the DIRECT link between deposit and withdrawal addresses, but they don't erase behavioral fingerprints — deposit/withdrawal timing correlation, amount matching, and address reuse elsewhere often let analysts probabilistically re-link funds. Full unlinkability requires far more discipline than most users apply in practice.

items.title: MEV: the tax you don't see on your transaction
items.body: Maximal extractable value (MEV) is profit block builders and searchers make by reordering, inserting, or censoring transactions within a block — commonly via sandwich attacks around large DEX swaps. It's a structural feature of public mempools, not a bug, and is one reason large trades are often routed through private order flow or MEV-protected RPCs.

items.title: What actually happens when you 'swap' on a DEX
items.body: A decentralized exchange swap doesn't match a buyer to a seller directly — it trades against a liquidity pool using an automated market maker formula (like Uniswap's constant-product x*y=k). Your trade size relative to pool depth determines your price impact, which is why a $500K swap on a shallow pool can move price far more than the same swap on a deep one.

items.title: Exchange inflows and outflows as a sentiment signal
items.body: Large transfers INTO exchange wallets are often read as sell pressure (coins typically move to an exchange to be liquidated), while transfers OUT are read as accumulation or self-custody. It's a heuristic, not proof — OTC desks, custody rebalancing and cold-storage rotations all produce the same on-chain shape without any trading intent.

items.title: Why address clustering matters more than balances
items.body: A single wallet's balance rarely tells the real story — most large holders spread funds across dozens of addresses to obscure size and intent. On-chain intelligence platforms use clustering heuristics (common-input-ownership, change-address detection, deposit-address fingerprinting) to link these addresses into one economic entity before flagging a 'whale.' That's why two wallets moving $60K each can be a single $120K whale move once clustered — and why raw explorer data alone under-counts real concentration.
